source: About Oscar Maiques, our lab at Barts Cancer Institute, and our research and teaching activities.
We connect tissue architecture with cancer biology, bringing experimental models, spatial analysis and AI together.
Established in April 2024, the mAIques Lab is led by Dr Oscar Maiques, Lecturer and Group Leader in Digital Pathology at Barts Cancer Institute, Queen Mary University of London.

We are based in the Centre for Cancer Biomarkers and Biotherapeutics. Our research investigates how the extracellular matrix and immune microenvironment influence cancer, with an emphasis on melanoma and pancreatic cancer.

Oscar trained in Biotechnology and completed his PhD at the University of Lleida with Prof Xavier Matias-Guiu and Prof Rosa Maria Marti. He subsequently undertook postdoctoral research with Prof Victoria Sanz-Moreno across King’s College London, Barts Cancer Institute and the Institute of Cancer Research.
He established the lab through the Barts Precision Medicine Programme, with mentorship from Prof Claude Chelala and Prof Carol Dezateux and support from Barts Charity.
Oscar teaches spatial biology, AI, personalised medicine and digital pathology, and supervises PhD, MSc and MRes research.
He co-leads Cancer Biology and Research Skills (SSC1b, CANM938) from 2026 and is a Fellow of the Higher Education Academy.

Oscar is a member of the British Association for Cancer Research and the European Association for Cancer Research, and the BCI delegate to the Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry Data Strategy and Capability Committee.
He contributes to tissue-bank application review, the BCI Communications Committee and the DERI Fellows Network.
We collaborate with Panakeia Technologies and contribute to the OPTIMA oncology network.
Patient involvement through the Pancreatic Cancer UK Research Involvement Network helps inform our research.

Cancer research in everyday language, patient and public involvement, and outreach at the mAIques Lab.
For patients, families, schools and anyone who is curious about our work.
A tumour is more than cancer cells. It also contains immune cells, blood vessels and a network of fibres that supports the tissue.

We study how these neighbours influence each other. The arrangement of cells and fibres may help explain why some cancers stay in one place while others spread. Our work focuses especially on melanoma, a type of skin cancer, and pancreatic cancer.
By understanding these relationships, we hope to find clues that could help researchers recognise more aggressive disease and develop better ways to study or treat it.
We use microscopes and special stains to see different kinds of cells and the fibres around them.
We grow cells in three-dimensional environments to explore how their surroundings change their behaviour.
We use computer tools, including artificial intelligence, to find patterns in tissue images and test whether those patterns are useful.
These are research studies. They do not currently provide an individual diagnostic test.
Living with cancer, caring for someone or supporting a family member brings knowledge that researchers need to hear.
We welcome conversations about the questions that matter to you, how we explain our work and how research could be more relevant to people affected by cancer.
It can mean commenting on a plain-language summary, discussing research priorities or helping us think about how to share results.
It is different from taking part in a clinical trial. You do not need a scientific background to start a conversation.
Interested in discussing cancer research, microscopes or AI with our team? Contact us to explore what might be possible.

What does AI do in our research?
AI helps us look for patterns in images and other research data. We test those patterns carefully; a computer prediction is not the same as a diagnosis.
